title: Lab 8 — Quiz 1
subtitle: Simple Stains — dyes, smears, positive and negative staining

questions.prompt: Identify the staining technique used on this slide: all cells are one color from a single dye.

options.text: Simple stain (crystal violet)
Gram stain (differential)
Negative stain (acidic dye)
Endospore stain (differential)

questions.explanation: Simple staining uses a single dye to stain all cells the same color (e.g., crystal violet, safranin).

why.B: A Gram stain uses several dyes and shows purple AND pink cells.
why.C: A negative stain colors the background, not the cells.
why.D: An endospore stain shows green spores and pink cells.

questions.prompt: Identify the staining technique: the background is dark and the cells are left unstained.

options.text: Positive simple stain
Acid-fast stain
Negative stain
Capsule stain

questions.explanation: Negative staining uses (commonly) an acidic dye that is repelled by the negatively charged cells, creating a dark background around clear cells.

why.A: Positive stains color the cells themselves.
why.B: Acid-fast stains color cells pink or blue.
why.D: This image shows a dark background with clear cells — a negative stain.

questions.prompt: This pathogenic yeast was prepared as a negative wet mount. Identify the organism.

options.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Candida albicans
Cryptococcus neoformans
Bacillus subtilis

questions.explanation: Negative wet mount examples: Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogenic yeast) and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast).

why.A: Saccharomyces (brewer's yeast) was the other negative wet mount example; this is the pathogenic yeast.
why.B: Candida was shown with crystal violet (positive stain).
why.D: B. subtilis is a rod-shaped bacterium.

questions.prompt: Which slide is viewed ONLY up to the 40X lens — never with oil immersion?

options.text: The positive stained bacteria (PB) slide
The positive stained yeast (PY) slide
The Gram-stained (G) smear slide
The negative wet mount (N slide)

questions.explanation: Focus up to 40X on the negative wet mount — do NOT use oil immersion on it. PB and PY are viewed at 100X oil.

why.A: PB is viewed under 100X oil immersion.
why.B: PY is viewed under 100X oil immersion.
why.C: Gram stains are viewed under oil immersion.

questions.prompt: Basic dyes used in positive staining are:

options.text: Anionic (negative) and repelled by negatively charged cells
Cationic (positive) and attracted to negatively charged cells
Cationic (positive) and repelled by positively charged cells
Neutral and absorbed through the cell wall

questions.explanation: Basic dyes are cationic (+), are attracted to negatively charged cells, stick and give them color. Positive staining = direct staining.

questions.prompt: Acidic dyes used in negative staining are:

options.text: Cationic (positive) and attracted to the cells
Anionic (negative) and attracted to the cells
Anionic (negative) and repelled by the negatively charged cells
Positively charged and used to color the cells

questions.explanation: Acidic dyes are anionic (−), are repelled by negatively charged cells, and often create a dark background. (Nuance: India ink is anionic but not acidic.)

questions.prompt: What are the three functions of heat fixing a smear?

options.text: Stains the cells, dries the smear, removes excess water
Kills the cells, adheres them to the slide, increases cell permeability
Sterilizes the slide, adds contrast, decolorizes the cells
Keeps the cells alive, adds color, and seals the coverslip

questions.explanation: Heat fixing: kills the cells, secures/adheres the specimen to the slide, and increases cell permeability.

why.A: Heat fixing comes after air drying and before staining.
why.C: Staining adds contrast; decolorizing is a Gram stain step.
why.D: Heat fixing kills the cells; wet mounts use coverslips.

questions.prompt: Why does a positive simple stain smear have to be heat fixed, but a negative wet mount does not?

options.text: The positive stain slide is rinsed; the wet mount is not
Negative stains only work on dead cells
Basic dyes only work at high temperatures
Yeasts can't be heat fixed

questions.explanation: Positive simple stains are rinsed, so the smear must be heat fixed first. Negative wet mounts aren't rinsed, so no heat fixing — the specimens are alive.

why.B: In wet mounts, cells are alive when viewed.
why.C: Heat fixing adheres cells so they survive rinsing.
why.D: Yeast PY smears are heat fixed for positive staining.

questions.prompt: How do you heat fix a dried smear?

options.text: Hold the smear inside the microincinerator for 10 seconds
Place the slide on the hot plate for 5 minutes
Smear facing away, pass the back of the slide past the microincinerator 3 times
Pass the smear side over a flame until it's dry

questions.explanation: Air dry first. Then, smear facing away, slowly pass the back of the slide left to right in front of the microincinerator opening 3 times. Let it cool.

why.A: Pass the back of the slide in front of the opening; don't put it inside.
why.B: Heating on the hot plate is for acid-fast/endospore staining.
why.D: Smears must air dry naturally first, then be heat fixed with the smear facing away.

questions.prompt: How long does the stain sit on the PB and PY slides during positive simple staining?

options.text: 10 seconds
1 minute
5 minutes
30 minutes

questions.explanation: Place the heat-fixed smear in the Coplin jar of stain for 1 minute, rinse both sides gently, then blot dry with bibulous paper (don't wipe).

why.A: 10 seconds is the Gram stain decolorizer time.
why.C: 5 minutes is the heat (mordant) time for acid-fast and endospore stains.
why.D: The basic dye penetrates for 1 minute.

questions.prompt: After rinsing a stained slide, how is it dried?

options.text: Wipe it dry with a Kimwipe
Pass it through the microincinerator
Gently blot with bibulous paper — do not wipe
Shake it dry over the sink

questions.explanation: Gently blot dry with bibulous paper; don't wipe and don't tear out pages.

why.A: Wiping removes the smear; blot instead.
why.B: Heat is for fixing before staining.
why.D: The protocol says to blot with bibulous paper.

questions.prompt: This Bacillus smear was stained blue with a single basic dye. Which dye was used?

options.text: Methylene blue
Crystal violet
Safranin
Malachite green

questions.explanation: Positive simple stain for Bacillus spp. with methylene blue.

why.D: Malachite green is the endospore primary stain.

questions.prompt: What is the clinical use of positive simple staining, as shown with Candida albicans here?

options.text: Viewing fungi in patients' specimens
Detecting acid-fast Mycobacterium
Determining Gram reaction for treatment
Viewing live, motile organisms

questions.explanation: Clinical relevance of positive simple staining: viewing fungi in patients' specimens.

why.C: The Gram stain determines the Gram reaction.
why.D: Positive stains are heat fixed, so the cells are dead.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of staining a smear?

options.text: To kill pathogens before the slide is thrown away
To make the cells grow larger and easier to see
To identify the species directly from the color
To increase contrast for better viewing under the microscope

questions.explanation: Staining increases contrast so specimens are easier to see.

why.A: Heat fixing kills cells; staining adds contrast.
why.C: Stains help distinguish cells, but staining's main purpose is contrast.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the negative wet mount is FALSE?

options.text: A loopful of stain is placed in the center of the slide
A generous loopful of organism is mixed into the dye
A coverslip is lowered at an angle
The specimens are alive when viewed
The mixture is smeared over the slide and heat fixed

questions.explanation: Do NOT smear the mixture over the slide, and wet mounts are not heat fixed.

why.A: True — stain goes on the center first.
why.C: True — touch the edge, then lower it slowly.
